lessons.title: Receiving raw materials
lessons.html:
Receiving raw materials

Feed quality starts at the gate. A feed mill cannot make good feed from bad raw materials. Receiving is the first and most important control point.

Receiving steps for bulk materials

  1. Documents: check the delivery note, order number, supplier, product and vehicle registration.
  2. Weighbridge: weigh the loaded truck in (gross mass).
  3. Sampling: take a representative sample with a probe from several points and depths of the load, following the sampling plan.
  4. Testing and grading: check smell, colour, temperature, insects, foreign material and moisture. The laboratory may test protein, mycotoxins and other parameters. Maize is graded against the grading regulations and the contract.
  5. Accept or reject: only accept loads that meet specification. Rejections are recorded and the supervisor informed.
  6. Off-load into the correct intake pit, with the route to the correct silo checked.
  7. Weigh out the empty truck (tare). Net mass is gross minus tare.

Warning signs at intake

  • Musty or sour smell, caking or visible mould, which point to mycotoxin risk.
  • Warm grain, which suggests heating from moisture or insects.
  • Live insects or rodent droppings.
  • Stones, glass, metal, plastic or treated (dyed) seed.
  • Wet loads or damaged tarpaulins.

Bagged and liquid materials

Premixes, vitamins, minerals, amino acids and medicaments arrive bagged or in containers. Check labels, batch numbers, expiry dates and packaging damage. Liquids such as molasses and fats are sampled and pumped into dedicated tanks. Every receipt is entered into the stock system so it can be traced.

Never let a truck off-load before acceptance is confirmed. Material in a silo cannot be removed easily, and one bad load can contaminate hundreds of tonnes of good grain.

lessons.title: Storage and warehousing practice
lessons.html:
Storage and warehousing practice

Bulk storage

  • Each silo or bin holds only its allocated ingredient. Labels on bins and in the control system must match.
  • Monitor grain temperature with probes or cables. Rising temperature means moisture migration, insects or mould. Aerate or turn the grain as instructed.
  • Fumigation of stored grain is done only by registered fumigators under strict controls. Nobody enters a fumigated area until it is declared safe.
  • Never enter a silo or bin without a confined space permit, harness, lifeline and standby person. Flowing grain can bury a person in seconds.

Warehouse layout and stock control

  • Store bags on pallets, off the floor and away from walls, so cleaning and inspection are possible.
  • Keep separate, marked areas for medicaments, premixes and general ingredients.
  • Use first-expired, first-out (FEFO) or first-in, first-out (FIFO) as the procedure says.
  • Quarantine area: suspect or rejected material is tagged and kept apart until a decision is made.
  • Stack heights are limited for safety and to protect bags at the bottom.

Pest control

Rodents, birds and insects damage and contaminate stock. Keep doors closed, clean spillage, seal holes, and use a documented pest control programme with mapped bait stations managed by trained staff. Never let rodenticide come into contact with ingredients.

Records and traceability

RecordPurpose
Goods received noteProof of what came in, from whom, when
Sample and lab resultsEvidence of quality at receipt
Bin or location recordWhich batch is where
Stock countBook stock versus physical stock

Good records let the mill trace a problem feed back to the raw material batch and supplier.

Key points

  • Check documents, weigh, sample, test, then accept or reject.
  • Mouldy, warm or infested material is a mycotoxin and quality risk.
  • Keep bins correctly allocated and labelled; monitor grain temperature.
  • Silos are confined spaces; enter only under permit.
  • Use FIFO or FEFO, quarantine suspect stock and keep traceable records.
